abstract.p: A fundamental challenge in reinforcement learning-based control is the development of interpretable policies that retain effective control performance under system uncertainty and nonlinear dynamics. To address this challenge, a domain-randomized deep Q-network (DQN) policy was distilled into a compact Takagi–Sugeno neuro-fuzzy Q-controller for reference tracking in an uncertain nonlinear mass–spring–damper system. A fixed-premise fuzzy inference structure was adopted, in which rule activation strengths and consequent parameters were used to compute action values directly, thereby enabling explicit examination of the learned decision mechanism without an additional opaque decision head. The proposed distillation framework was evaluated against a directly trained neuro-fuzzy controller with an identical architecture. Closed-loop tracking performance, teacher–student action agreement, and rule-pruning fidelity were systematically assessed under nominal, robust, and stress conditions, using ten independent random seeds and 160 matched evaluation scenarios per operating regime. For the distilled controller with seven membership functions (7MFs) per input, the mean absolute tracking errors were 0.1589, 0.1552, and 0.3437, respectively, compared with 0.4989, 0.4299, and 0.5690 for its directly trained counterpart. Teacher–student action agreement decreased from under nominal conditions to under stress conditions. Rule-pruning analysis further demonstrated that a reduced controller retaining 64 of the original 343 fuzzy rules preserved of the full student’s action selections. State-space and trajectory-level analyses were conducted to characterize policy disagreement and its observed association with tracking degradation. Although the distilled neuro-fuzzy controller outperformed a manually designed fuzzy controller, its tracking accuracy remained lower than that achieved by proportional–integral–derivative (PID) control, linear quadratic regulator (LQR) control, and the original DQN teacher. The resulting framework provides a basis for evaluating explainable policy compression in uncertain nonlinear control systems without implying guaranteed closed-loop stability or superior tracking performance.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Deep reinforcement learning can learn feedback policies for uncertain nonlinear dynamics, and domain randomization exposes policies to variations in system parameters during training. Generalization and safety, nevertheless, remain open under distribution shift [1], [2], [3], [4]. A separate deployment obstacle is that neural action values do not explain which measured quantities drive a decision. Reviews of explainable reinforcement learning distinguish an intrinsically readable policy from a post-hoc account of an opaque one [5], [6].

Fuzzy controllers can expose antecedents and consequents, although their interpretability depends on premise design, rule usage, and the operating distribution [7]. Type-2 fuzzy and adaptive neuro-fuzzy sliding-mode controllers have been developed for uncertain surgical-robot tracking [8], [9]; a newer actor–critic sliding-mode approach also provides a Lyapunov analysis for nonlinear systems [10]. Directly trained neuro-fuzzy reinforcement-learning controllers address mobile-robot and other control tasks [11], [12], while a compact neuro-fuzzy method addresses measurement noise [13]. These studies motivate interpretable control but do not establish how faithfully a compressed deep Q-network (DQN) reproduces decisions across sparsely visited states or how that fidelity affects tracking.

The distillation of DQN policies into neuro-fuzzy models is not itself novel. Gevaert et al. [14] demonstrated this approach on benchmarks and compared learning with direct fuzzy control, while Xu et al. [15] extracted interpretable fuzzy rules and evaluated temporal fidelity. Recent concept-based distillation methods have produced sparse surrogate models for image-based policies, whereas temporal distillation methods have compressed both policy representations and their action timing [16]. Those studies target different settings and measures. For uncertain physical tracking, aggregate agreement alone cannot reveal where policy compression fails, whether disagreement affects closed-loop error, or whether teacher guidance changes the rule base relative to direct training. Furthermore, the existing studies do not eliminate the need to distinguish empirical tracking from a formal stability guarantee.
This study contributes the following evidence, without claiming priority for the distillation algorithm itself:

(i) A fixed-premise, head-free Takagi–Sugeno–Kang (TSK) Q-controller whose rule contributions can be inspected, together with an explicit analysis of how action-value errors can change a discrete decision.
(ii) A held-out, common-trace evaluation across nominal, robust, and stress regimes that combines spatial and visitation-conditioned imitation measures with paired closed-loop tracking outcomes.

(iii) An architecture-matched, reward-only comparator with seven membership function (7MF) per input and a post-hoc pruning analysis that test whether teacher supervision changes accuracy and preservation of the learned fuzzy decisions. The 130 reward-training episodes are matched; offline labels, interactions, and computation are not.
The objective of this study is to measure the utility and limitations of interpretable compression rather than to claim the best tracking controller.

sec.title: 2.1. End-to-end control and learning workflow
sec.p: Figure 1 distinguishes the physical system from the learning roles. The mass–spring–damper is the controlled plant, while the teacher refers to the DQN policy and the student to its TSK Q-controller approximation, rather than to two different plants. Both policies use the same clipped, noisy observation construction and select a force from the same discrete set. A domain-randomized simulator first trains the teacher, whose visited states provide action, distribution, and Q-value targets for offline student distillation. This is followed by reward-based fine-tuning of the student. An identical TSK architecture is trained directly using reward signals as a comparator. Frozen policies are then evaluated on matched held-out scenarios; teacher-visited states support fidelity analysis, while separate closed-loop rollouts support tracking and pruning analyses.

The mass–spring–damper is the physical plant; teacher and student are policies for that same plant. The teacher is trained for 100 reward episodes and provides 8,192 labeled states for 70 offline student epochs. The student is subsequently fine-tuned for 30 reward episodes. The direct 7MF comparator receives 130 reward episodes without teacher targets. Common-trace held-out evaluation distinguishes fidelity on teacher-visited states from closed-loop tracking, rule explanations, and pruning. Episode counts are matched in terms of reward training rather than total interactions or computation.

The reported pruning fidelity is pooled across all three regimes for each seed; it is not a regime-specific quantity. Rule ranking and pruned-policy evaluation use the same held-out scenario collection. Therefore, pruning is presented as a post-hoc operating-envelope analysis rather than independent validation on a second scenario set.

sec.title: 2.8. Experimental protocol
sec.p: All final experiments use seeds 0–9. Each seed contains 16 independently sampled scenarios in each evaluation regime, giving 160 rollouts per controller and regime. For a given seed–regime–scenario tuple, every controller receives the same initial condition, plant parameters, reference, disturbance trace, and observation-noise trace. This pairing prevents exogenous variation from being mistaken for a controller effect. Evaluation regimes are held out from training and use the ranges in Table 1.

Baselines are a hand-crafted two-input fuzzy controller, a proportional–integral–derivative (PID) controller (
K p
= 35,
K d
= 8,
K i
= 2), a nominal discrete-time linear quadratic regulator (LQR), the domain-randomized DQN teacher, distilled five-membership-function and 7MF students, a 7MF student trained without domain randomization, and a directly trained 7MF model. The PID and LQR controllers are deliberately strong for this mechanical tracking problem; they prevent improvements in interpretability from being presented as optimal control performance.
The primary metric is mean absolute tracking error:

Secondary metrics include root mean square error, integrated absolute error, the discrete-time integral of squared force (control energy), settled fraction, and failure rate. CIs are computed from the ten seed-level means using the critical value of Student’s $t$-distribution with nine degrees of freedom. Paired comparisons first average scenario differences within each seed and then apply a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test over ten seed differences. The three direct-versus-distilled regime tests are corrected using the Holm method. Scenario-level win rates and pooled Spearman tests are descriptive complements; the inferential unit for the main performance comparison remains the seed.

Figure 3 shows the spatial structure hidden by the averages. Nominal and robust teacher trajectories concentrate along a narrow error--error-rate manifold, while stress trajectories spread farther from it. The integral input is included in the fidelity calculation but marginalized in this visualization.

sec.title: 3.2. Closed-loop performance
sec.p: Figure 5 shows the scenario-level MAE distributions. The MAEs for the distilled 7MF controller are 0.1589 (95% CI half-width: 0.0178), 0.1552 (0.0175), and 0.3437 (0.0284) across the three regimes. The hand-crafted fuzzy controller obtains 0.2572, 0.2558, and 0.4463. Therefore, the distilled 7MF controller reduces the MAEs by 38.2%, 39.4%, and 23.0%. None of the unpruned controllers in Figure 5 produces a displacement failure.

caption.title: Closed-loop distributions over ten seeds and 160 held-out scenarios per regime

sec.p: The interpretability cost remains visible. The PID controller achieves MAEs of 0.1317, 0.1363, and 0.2710; the nominal LQR achieves 0.0471, 0.0702, and 0.1977; and the DQN teacher achieves 0.0748, 0.0742, and 0.2200. Accordingly, the proposed student is not the most accurate controller for this plant. Its value is the combination of improved fuzzy control, explicit rules, and measurable compression. Mean control energy values are 107.5, 114.5, and 274.0 for the distilled 7MF policy, compared with 850.1, 830.7, and 989.4 for the directly trained 7MF policy; under the tested schedules, distillation improves tracking and reduces across-seed outcome variability rather than merely trading error for more actuation.

Direct training produces a markedly less prune-tolerant policy under this operating-envelope analysis. Its pooled fidelity is only 42.8% at 64 rules, 57.2% at 96 rules, and 66.4% at 128 rules. sec.title: 3.4. Rule-level interpretability
sec.p:
The full 7MF grid contains 343 antecedent combinations, but the distilled student uses only 27.2
±
0.4 effective rules, with approximately 3.15 rules exceeding the instantaneous activation threshold per state and 9.9%
±
1.5 percentage points of the rule base covered. The directly trained 7MF controller uses approximately 30.1 effective rules, 3.44 active rules per state, and 23.8% coverage. Similar effective counts therefore do not imply similar rule allocation or pruning tolerance (Figure 7).

Figure 8 illustrates the explanation interface for the final seed-0 distilled 7MF checkpoint. Mean firing ranks globally used rules over the held-out common-trace scenarios, while the trajectory view reports the leading local activations together with the selected force for nominal scenario 0. A single rule should not be read as a complete causal explanation because the final Q-values aggregate all normalized firings. Reporting the leading rules, their strengths, and the final action preserves that distinction.

caption.title: Intrinsic rule-level explanation for the final seed-0 distilled 7MF checkpoint

sec.p: The same final seed-0 policy can be audited globally by fixing the integral input at zero and sweeping error and error rate (Figure 9). The surface reveals switching boundaries and sign structure that are inaccessible from an aggregate score. It is a diagnostic visualization rather than a stability certificate.

sec.title: 4.1. Fidelity and closed-loop consequences
sec.p: The discrete argmax in Eq. (12) makes action agreement sensitive to the gap between the best and second-best action values. The decision-margin condition is sufficient but was not evaluated as a certified margin on every rollout; the mismatch maps instead provide empirical localization. Action agreement in the stress regime decreases from 59.8% under nominal conditions to 29.8%, while the softened KL divergence increases from 0.0628 to 0.1821. The student–teacher MAE gap also grows from 0.0841 m under nominal conditions to 0.1237 m under stress conditions. These concurrent changes are consistent with the shifted occupancy and stronger uncertainty, but they do not isolate a single cause.

Action agreement is not itself a measure of control performance. The five-membership-function student agrees more often with its teacher than the 7MF student in nominal and robust conditions (65.2% versus 59.8%, and 60.4% versus 53.3%), yet yields higher MAEs (0.1818 versus 0.1589, and 0.1780 versus 0.1552). Conversely, a few high-disagreement scenarios retain nearly the same MAEs because different force sequences can have limited net effect or can be corrected later. The positive associations between disagreement and MAE are observational: difficult scenarios can increase both quantities. The nominal density-quartile pattern is also non-monotonic, indicating that low visitation alone does not explain each mismatch.

sec.title: 4.2. Benefits and cost of teacher guidance
sec.p: Compared with the directly trained 7MF controller with the same architecture, distillation reduces MAEs by 68.1%, 63.9%, and 39.6% in nominal, robust, and stress conditions. The ten-seed paired differences remain significant after Holm correction. The distilled policy also uses less measured control energy and shows narrower across-seed MAE intervals. However, neither result implies that it is the best controller, as the PID controller, the LQR, and the DQN teacher are more accurate in every regime. The comparison matches the fuzzy architecture and 130 reward-training episodes, not total simulator interactions, optimizer updates, or computation. Thus, the result supports an advantage of the complete teacher-guided schedule tested in this study rather than a claim of superiority under matched computational budgets.

The pruning result provides an additional structural observation. Retaining 64 of 343 rules (18.7%) preserves 90.5% of full-student actions, with MAE increases of 0.0090, 0.0067, and 0.0083 m across the three regimes. A directly trained model retains only 66.4% of its actions with 128 rules and has two stress failures after pruning. Similar full-model effective-rule counts therefore conceal different allocations of decision weight. The action-margin condition explains why rule removal can be harmless where the value gap is large, but the condition was not used to certify these pruned trajectories. The observed MAE changes do not establish equivalence.

sec.title: 4.3. Novelty and validity limits
sec.p: Gevaert et al. [14] investigated the distillation of DQN policies into neuro-fuzzy models on benchmark tasks, while Xu et al. [15] investigated interpretable fuzzy-rule extraction. The present study extends these approaches through an integrated evaluation of uncertain nonlinear tracking, teacher-visited-state fidelity, paired closed-loop outcomes, and architecture-matched pruning. Concept-based and temporal distillation pursue different compression objectives [16]. Unlike control designs with a Lyapunov analysis [10], the present policy has no proved stability, robust invariance, or safety guarantee.

The evidence covers one simulated plant family, one discrete force set, and ten seeds. The fixed premise grid can limit transfer outside its linguistic domain. Teacher-visited-state fidelity omits states reached only by the student; two-dimensional maps marginalize the integral input, and density quartiles depend on binning. Pruning ranks and evaluates rules on the same held-out scenarios, indicating that it is a post-hoc operating-envelope result rather than independent validation. Hardware experiments, training under matched computational budgets, and independent pruning scenarios are needed before generalizing the reported gains.

sec.title: 5. Conclusion
sec.p:
A fixed-premise TSK Q-controller can compress a DQN policy into directly inspectable rule–action values, but the resulting behavior must be assessed in a closed loop. Across nominal, robust, and stress regimes, the distilled 7MF policy achieved MAEs of 0.1589, 0.1552, and 0.3437 m. These values were 68.1%, 63.9%, and 39.6% lower than those of the architecture-matched, directly trained 7MF controller, which achieved MAEs of 0.4989, 0.4299, and 0.5690 m under the tested schedules; paired ten-seed comparisons remained significant after Holm correction (
p
adj
≤
0.006). Relative to a manual fuzzy controller, the corresponding reductions were 38.2%, 39.4%, and 23.0%. Pruning to 64 of 343 rules preserved 90.5% of full-student actions, although the MAE increased slightly. The distillation was not lossless: teacher-action agreement was only 29.8% under stress conditions, while the PID controller, the LQR, and the DQN teacher remained more accurate. The result is an auditable policy with quantified trade-offs between accuracy and fidelity, rather than a stability guarantee.

Future work should test additional plants and continuous-action policies, compare matched total computation and simulator interactions, and validate rule pruning on independent shifted scenarios. Hardware-in-the-loop studies and safety constraints or formal stability analysis are needed before deployment.
